You previously formulated the following research problem for the target paper.

Research problem: In MVFA's few-shot mode, the released code defines a K-shot support set as K normal and K abnormal target-domain images, the abnormal ones loaded with expert pixel masks, and uses them both to fine-tune the adapters (Dice, Focal and BCE losses) and to fill the memory bank. Can the K real abnormal images with masks be replaced by synthetic abnormal images made from the K normal supports alone — lesion-like patches cut from other normal images of the same modality, intensity-perturbed and Poisson-blended into the support, with the pasted region as the free mask — and how much of the few-shot image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO of real-abnormal MVFA does this normal-only variant keep on each BMAD dataset for K in {2, 4, 8, 16}? A memory-bank-only variant (no fine-tuning on target data) is reported as the lower reference.
Rationale: L4 and L18, confirmed in the released code, show that 'K = 4' means four normal plus four expertly delineated abnormal slices, the most expensive annotation in medical imaging, and the paper never measures what those abnormal images and masks contribute. Several related methods show that synthetic anomalies can stand in for real ones when adapting CLIP to medical images (MediCLIP [22], AnomaMed's anomaly blending [53], the UWF framework's Poisson blending [43], LesionPaste [32]), and [55] shows that selecting informative synthetic images matters; but none of them measures the gap to real abnormal supervision inside the same adapter, on the same support set, under an unseen-modality protocol. The question isolates one component — the abnormal half of MVFA's few-shot support set — keeps architecture, losses and evaluation unchanged, and needs only image operations on data that BMAD already provides, so it is feasible on one GPU; its answer tells a hospital whether MVFA's few-shot mode can be used before any abnormal case has been annotated.

ReviewingAgents evaluated it on five criteria. Their reviews, feedback, and ratings are:
- Clarity: rating 4/5. Review: The component (the abnormal half of the K-shot support set), the replacement and the outcomes are stated, and the memory-bank-only lower reference is useful. The synthesis recipe is described loosely: patch size and shape, the intensity perturbation and how many synthetic images are made per support are not given, and it is unclear whether synthetic images also enter the memory bank. Feedback: Fix the synthesis parameters (e.g., elliptical patches of 2-15% of the image area, one synthetic image per normal support and epoch) and state that the memory bank keeps only real normal supports.
- Relevance: rating 4/5. Review: Directly addresses L4 and L18: the released code confirms that K-shot means K expertly masked abnormal images, the costliest annotation, and the paper never measures their contribution. Feedback: Frame the outcome as the annotation cost that the synthetic variant removes per target site.
- Originality: rating 3/5. Review: Synthetic anomalies for adapting CLIP to medical images are already common ([22], [32], [43], [53], [55]). The contribution is a controlled measurement — synthetic versus real abnormal supports inside the same adapter, with the same support set and protocol — which is useful but not a new method. Feedback: Sharpen the question with a hypothesis that the literature does not settle, e.g., that the gap depends on lesion size or modality (focal BrainMRI/LiverCT lesions versus diffuse ChestXray/HIS findings).
- Feasibility: rating 4/5. Review: Only image operations on data BMAD already provides, the existing losses and the same training budget as the original few-shot runs; 4 K values x 6 datasets x 3 seeds x 3 draws is a sizeable but manageable grid on one GPU. Poisson blending needs care on single-channel images. Feedback: Reduce the grid if needed by running K in {2, 8} for all datasets and the full K range on two datasets.
- Significance: rating 3/5. Review: Practically relevant for deployment at a new site, but the expected outcome — synthetic anomalies recover part of the gain — is close to what [22] and [55] already report, so the result is likely to be incremental unless the modality dependence is analysed. Feedback: Tie the result to a concrete decision rule (when real abnormal annotations are worth collecting).

Revise the research problem so that it addresses the feedback while keeping what the reviewers rated highly. Keep it a single, fine-grained, to-the-point problem that still addresses the same limitations, respects the constraints below, and stays centred on the target paper.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- L3. The 'zero-shot' protocol is not supervision-free: adapters are trained on labeled medical images (and dense masks) from the five remaining datasets, with per-fold source budgets unreported, and the resulting model is compared against a training-free baseline (WinCLIP). 'Zero-shot' here means only that the target modality/anatomy is unseen; the source pool includes thousands of normal images plus labeled subsets (83-1,490 labeled images per dataset) and the leave-one-out folds differ greatly in size, so the reported 20.34-point AC gain over WinCLIP compares a heavily supervised model with an unsupervised one and the 'lightweight' framing is unsupported. The zero-shot numbers therefore do not establish transfer without medical labels. Code check (released MVFA code): In the released code every source image trains the detection adapters with an image-level BCE loss, while the segmentation adapters, which produce the anomaly maps, are trained with Dice and Focal losses only on the datasets that have masks.
- L4. The few-shot protocol is under-specified: the paper never states the normal/anomalous composition of the K labeled samples, whether K counts total images or images per class, how subsets are seeded, or whether the K target samples are used alone or together with labeled data from the other five datasets. The appendix only says a 'random subset of labeled training samples' is drawn from a pool containing both normal and anomalous images. If a K=2 draw contains no anomaly, the claimed benefit of abnormal supervision disappears; if cross-dataset labeled data is also used, MVFA is not a pure few-shot target-domain learner and the comparison with baselines trained on K target samples is unfair. The protocol therefore cannot be replicated or interpreted, and the shot-count trends are uninterpretable. Code check (released MVFA code): The released code answers this: 'K-shot' means K normal AND K abnormal images, the abnormal ones with pixel masks, both drawn from BMAD's valid/ split, from one fixed file per dataset and shot number.
- L5. The multi-level alignment loss applies Dice and Focal losses against pixel masks at every level to all datasets, yet OCT17, ChestXray and HIS provide only image-level labels and the treatment of the missing masks is never specified. The loss definition requires a ground-truth mask S for every training tuple, so for the three image-label-only datasets the segmentation terms are either ill-defined, silently dropped, or replaced by undocumented pseudo-masks. This makes the numbers on half the benchmark non-reproducible, means the effective objective differs across folds, and means the segmentation branch is validated on only BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC — so the claim of one universal AC+AS model is unsupported for image-label-only data. Code check (released MVFA code): In the released code the Dice and Focal losses are applied only to datasets with masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC); OCT17, ChestXray and HIS train only the detection adapters; no pseudo-masks are used.
- L18. The few-shot protocol still requires expert pixel-level lesion masks for BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC (83, 166 and 115 labeled images annotated with segmentation masks), and the annotation cost, the number of masks needed, and performance without masks are never quantified. The problem formulation makes a full pixel mask part of every training tuple, so 'K=4' means four expertly delineated slices rather than four cheap labels — the most expensive annotation type in medical imaging. Since real deployments typically have only a handful of image-level labels, the practical advantage over normal-only training is overstated in settings where dense masks are expensive, and the paper's scarce-data motivation is not addressed. Code check (released MVFA code): Confirmed in the released code: the K abnormal support images are loaded together with their masks.
Constraints:
- The problem will be investigated by a student team in the next few weeks by modifying the public code of the target paper (https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD) and evaluating on the public BMAD benchmark (brain MRI, liver CT, retinal OCT: RESC and OCT17, chest X-ray, histopathology), using a single Google Colab Pro GPU (A100 40GB or L4 24GB). No new clinical data can be collected and no new expert annotations can be made.
- Shared evaluation protocol (from the limitation group 'Leakage-free generalisation protocol': L1, L2, L11, L20, L22, L27, L37, C2): checkpoints and hyper-parameters are selected on a held-out validation split of the SOURCE modalities and never on the target test set, and the MVFA baseline is re-run under the same rule; results are reported under a modality-disjoint leave-one-modality-out split (RESC and OCT17 are held out together, never one with the other in training), with patient-level separation where identifiers exist, over at least 3 random seeds and 3 few-shot support draws with mean and standard deviation, and with a simple supervised baseline trained on the same labelled images (L31) where relevant.

Problem: In MVFA's few-shot mode, the released code defines a K-shot support set as K normal and K abnormal target-domain images, the abnormal ones with expert pixel masks, used to fine-tune the adapters (Dice, Focal and BCE losses), while the memory bank holds the normal supports. Can the K real abnormal images with masks be replaced by synthetic abnormal images built from the K normal supports alone, and does the size of the gap depend on the type of lesion? Synthesis: one synthetic image per normal support and epoch, made by Poisson-blending an elliptical patch (2-15% of the image area) cut from a different normal image of the same modality, with random intensity scaling, the pasted region serving as the mask; the memory bank keeps only real normal supports. Outcomes per BMAD dataset for K in {2, 8} (full range K in {2, 4, 8, 16} on BrainMRI and ChestXray): few-shot image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO of the synthetic variant relative to real-abnormal MVFA, with a memory-bank-only variant as the lower reference. Hypothesis: the synthetic variant recovers most of the gain on focal-lesion datasets (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC) and little on diffuse-finding datasets (ChestXray, HIS, OCT17).

Rationale: L4 and L18, confirmed in the released code, show that 'K = 4' means four normal plus four expertly delineated abnormal slices, and the paper never measures what those abnormal images contribute. Synthetic anomalies are a known substitute when adapting CLIP to medical images (MediCLIP [22], LesionPaste [32], the UWF framework's Poisson blending [43], AnomaMed [53]), and [55] shows that the choice of synthetic images matters; but none measures the gap to real abnormal supervision inside the same adapter with the same support set, and none asks for which kinds of medical anomaly the substitution fails. The question isolates the abnormal half of the support set, keeps architecture, losses and evaluation unchanged, needs only image operations on BMAD data, and is sized to one GPU; its answer is a decision rule for a new site: when collecting K annotated abnormal cases is worth the expert time.
